column2: Lying on your left or right side is safe; waking up on your back at night isn't a problem — just turn onto your side.
Frequent peeing, leg cramps and heartburn can disrupt sleep.
Fall asleep on your side; you can use a pregnancy pillow for support.
Drink a little less in the evening, but keep drinking enough during the day.
Take short daytime naps; keep a regular sleep schedule.
If you notice fewer baby movements: see a doctor the same day.
If loud snoring or pauses in breathing during sleep are noticed.
If sleeplessness seriously affects your daily life.
Stopping breastfeeding (weaning)
Stopping breastfeeding gradually is more comfortable for both mother and baby.
The WHO recommends only breast milk for the first 6 months, then breastfeeding alongside solid foods up to 2 years and beyond.
Stopping suddenly increases the risk of engorgement and mastitis.
When to stop is a decision specific to each mother and baby.
Drop one feed every 3–5 days; start with the one the baby is least interested in.
Replace breastfeeding with moments of closeness such as cuddles and reading.
If your breasts feel full, express just enough milk to feel comfortable and apply something cold.
Remember that babies under 12 months need formula in place of breast milk.
Redness, hardness, pain and fever in the breast (possible mastitis).
If the baby refuses formula or other foods and isn't gaining weight.
If the mother feels marked sadness or anxiety during weaning.
Postpartum hair loss
Heavy hair shedding starting 2–4 months after birth is common and usually temporary.
Hair that didn't fall out during pregnancy sheds after birth as hormones change.
Shedding usually eases within 6–12 months and hair grows back.
Iron deficiency and thyroid problems can increase shedding.
Don't tie your hair tightly; brush gently.
Eat a balanced diet; pay attention to iron and protein intake.
If your doctor recommended it, continue postnatal vitamin supplements.
If shedding lasts longer than a year or there are bald patches.
If thyroid signs such as extreme tiredness, palpitations or weight change come with it.
Febrile seizure (fever fit)
As fever rises, some children aged 6 months to 5 years may have a brief seizure; it's frightening but mostly harmless.
The seizure usually lasts a few minutes; the child stiffens or jerks, the eyes may roll and they may not respond.
In some children who've had a febrile seizure it can happen again.
Fever medicines improve comfort but haven't been shown to prevent seizures.
Stay calm; lay the child on the floor on their side and move hard objects away.
Don't put anything in their mouth, and don't try to hold them down or shake them.
Note the time the seizure started; film it if you can.
After the seizure the child may be sleepy; stay with them.
If it's the first seizure: see a doctor.
If the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes, or there's difficulty breathing or bluish colour: call 112.
Stiff neck, vomiting, a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, or the child is hard to wake: call 112.
Nosebleeds are common in children and most stop within 10–15 minutes with correct pressure.
Dry air, nose picking and colds are the most common causes.
Bleeding usually comes from small vessels at the front of the nose.
Sit the child up and tilt their head slightly forward; don't tip it back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose with two fingers for 10 minutes without letting go.
Tell them to breathe through the mouth and spit out blood rather than swallow it.
Humidify the room in winter.
If it hasn't stopped despite 20 minutes of pressure: go to A&E.
If it happened after a head injury or is very heavy: go to A&E.
If it keeps recurring, or comes with easy bruising or bleeding gums: see a doctor.
Insect stings and animal bites
Most insect stings cause local swelling and itching; animal bites, however, should always be assessed.
After a bee sting the stinger may stay in the skin.
Some people can develop a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a sting.
Cat, dog and other animal bites carry a risk of infection and rabies.
Remove a bee stinger by scraping it out with a fingernail or card; don't squeeze it with tweezers.
Wash the area with soapy water and apply something cold.
Wash an animal bite with plenty of soapy water for at least 15 minutes and go to a health facility the same day.
Protect children from mosquitoes with age-appropriate repellent and suitable clothing.
Swelling of the face or lips, shortness of breath, widespread redness or fainting: call 112 immediately.
A sting inside the mouth or on the neck: go to A&E.
Any animal bite or scratch: go to a health facility the same day (rabies assessment).
Electric shock and home electrical safety
Sockets, cables and chargers are risky for young children; in a shock, cut the power first.
An electric shock can cause internal burns and heart rhythm problems even if it looks minor outside.
The risk is higher in wet areas such as bathrooms and kitchens.
Before touching the person, switch off the fuse or unplug the device.
If the power can't be cut, move the person away with a non-conducting object such as wood.
Fit socket covers, keep cables out of reach and don't leave chargers plugged in.
Make sure your home has a residual-current device (RCD).
After any electric shock, go to a health facility even if the child seems fine.
Loss of consciousness, not breathing, burns or palpitations: call 112 immediately.
